claim: Small RNA sequencing was performed on human lymphatic endothelial cells (HMVEC-dLy) and human blood endothelial cells (HUVEC) using triplicate samples.
source: We performed small RNA sequencing on human lymphatic endothelial cells (LEC) and human blood endothelial cells (BEC) to identify microRNAs enriched in LECs compared to BECs. We used triplicate samples of total RNA isolated from human dermal lymphatic microvascular endothelial cells (HMVEC-dLy, representing LEC) and human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVEC, representing BEC) for sequencing (Figure 1a).
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental methodology used for small RNA sequencing, including the specific cell types and number of replicates.

claim: HMVEC-dLy express higher levels of lymphatic markers PROX1, FLT4, and PDPN compared to HUVEC.
source: HMVEC-dLy express higher levels of PROX1, FLT4, and PDPN, while HUVEC showed enrichment for NR2F2, KDR, CDH5, and EGFL7, showing that these cell types appropriately express genes representative of lymphatic or blood vessel identity (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by TaqMan quantitative RT-PCR measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: HUVEC showed enrichment for blood vascular markers NR2F2, KDR, CDH5, and EGFL7 compared to HMVEC-dLy.
source: HMVEC-dLy express higher levels of PROX1, FLT4, and PDPN, while HUVEC showed enrichment for NR2F2, KDR, CDH5, and EGFL7, showing that these cell types appropriately express genes representative of lymphatic or blood vessel identity (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by TaqMan quantitative RT-PCR measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: A total of ~10 million reads were collected for each RNAseq sample.
source: A total of ~10 million reads were collected for each RNAseq sample and the sequences were aligned using the miRbase v22 (Kozomara and Griffiths-Jones, 2014).
evidence: The manuscript states the number of sequencing reads obtained per sample.

claim: 445 annotated microRNAs remained after filtering out microRNAs with less than 10 reads in three or more samples.
source: We excluded from further analysis any microRNAs that were represented by less than 10 reads in three or more of the six (two triplicate) sequenced samples, resulting in 445 annotated microRNAs.
evidence: The manuscript describes the filtering criteria and resulting number of microRNAs analyzed.

claim: 98 microRNAs showed a significant difference between LEC and BEC samples (p<0.01, FDR < 0.01).
source: 98 of these microRNAs showed a significant difference between the LEC and BEC samples (p<0.01, false discovery rate (FDR) < 0.01).
evidence: The manuscript reports the number of significantly differentially expressed microRNAs with statistical thresholds.

claim: 30 microRNAs were highly enriched in LECs (fold change >4).
source: From the 98 microRNAs we identified 30 that were highly enriched in LECs (fold change (FC) >4) and 20 that were highly enriched in BECs (FC >4) (Figure 1a and Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports the number of highly enriched microRNAs in LECs based on fold change criteria, with data shown in Figure 1a.

claim: 20 microRNAs were highly enriched in BECs (fold change >4).
source: From the 98 microRNAs we identified 30 that were highly enriched in LECs (fold change (FC) >4) and 20 that were highly enriched in BECs (FC >4) (Figure 1a and Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports the number of highly enriched microRNAs in BECs based on fold change criteria, with data shown in Figure 1a.

claim: miR-204-5p was the most highly enriched microRNA in LEC, with 105-fold higher representation compared to BEC.
source: Among the 30 LEC-enriched microRNAs, miR-204–5 p was by far the most highly enriched in LEC, with 105-fold higher representation in the LEC sequences compared to BEC (Figure 1b).
evidence: The manuscript reports the fold enrichment of miR-204-5p in LECs based on sequencing data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: miR-204-5p is very highly enriched in LEC compared to BEC as confirmed by TaqMan microRNA qPCR assay.
source: Using the TaqMan microRNA qPCR assay, we confirmed that miR-204–5 p is very highly enriched in LEC compared to BEC, in contrast to previously reported vascular microRNAs miR-126 and miR-31 that are more highly enriched in BEC (Figure 1c).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR validation data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: miR-126 and miR-31 are more highly enriched in BEC compared to LEC.
source: Using the TaqMan microRNA qPCR assay, we confirmed that miR-204–5 p is very highly enriched in LEC compared to BEC, in contrast to previously reported vascular microRNAs miR-126 and miR-31 that are more highly enriched in BEC (Figure 1c).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: Zebrafish mir-204 is highly enriched in EGFP-sorted lymphatic cells compared to mCherry-sorted arterial and double-sorted venous cells.
source: Using these sorted endothelial cell populations we were able to show that zebrafish mir-204 is highly enriched in EGFP-sorted lymphatic cells, while the blood endothelial microRNAs mir-126 and mir-31 are more enriched in mCherry-positive or double-positive BECs (Figure 1f).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data from FACS-sorted zebrafish endothelial cells shown in Figure 1f.

claim: Zebrafish mir-126 and mir-31 are more enriched in mCherry-positive or double-positive blood endothelial cells.
source: Using these sorted endothelial cell populations we were able to show that zebrafish mir-204 is highly enriched in EGFP-sorted lymphatic cells, while the blood endothelial microRNAs mir-126 and mir-31 are more enriched in mCherry-positive or double-positive BECs (Figure 1f).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data from FACS-sorted zebrafish endothelial cells shown in Figure 1f.

claim: miR-204 is a highly conserved microRNA enriched in the lymphatic endothelium in both humans and zebrafish.
source: These data show that miR-204 is a highly conserved microRNA enriched in the lymphatic endothelium in both humans and zebrafish.
evidence: The claim is based on the sequencing and qPCR data from both human and zebrafish cells presented in the manuscript.

claim: Human miR-204 is located in the sixth intron of TRPM3.
source: Human miR-204 is located in the sixth intron of TRPM3 (Transient Receptor Potential Cation Channel Subfamily M Member 3), and the mature microRNA is 100% conserved amongst a variety of vertebrate species (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: The manuscript states the genomic location of human miR-204, with a schematic shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1a.

claim: The mature miR-204 sequence is 100% conserved amongst a variety of vertebrate species.
source: Human miR-204 is located in the sixth intron of TRPM3 (Transient Receptor Potential Cation Channel Subfamily M Member 3), and the mature microRNA is 100% conserved amongst a variety of vertebrate species (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: The manuscript states the conservation of miR-204 sequence, with alignment shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1a.

claim: The zebrafish genome contains three paralogues of mir-204.
source: The zebrafish genome contains three paralogues of mir-204 (miRBase.org).
evidence: The manuscript states the number of mir-204 paralogues in zebrafish, citing miRBase.org as the source.

claim: One zebrafish mir-204 is found in intron 5 of the trpm3 gene (mir-204-1).
source: As in the human genome, one mir-204 is found in intron 5 of the zebrafish trpm3 gene (mir-204–1) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: The manuscript describes the genomic location of zebrafish mir-204-1, with a schematic shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Additional zebrafish mir-204 sequences are found in intron 5 of trpm1a (mir-204-2) and in intron 4 of trpm1b (mir-204-3).
source: However, additional zebrafish mir-204 sequences are also found in intron 5 of trpm1a and in intron 4 of trpm1b (mir-204–2 and mir-204–3, respectively; Figure 2—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: The manuscript describes the genomic locations of zebrafish mir-204-2 and mir-204-3, with schematics shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1b.

claim: The mature mir-204 sequences from all three zebrafish copies are 100% identical.
source: Although each of the three copies of mir-204 in the zebrafish has unique precursor sequences, their mature mir-204 sequences are 100% identical (Figure 2a).
evidence: The manuscript states the identity of mature sequences, with alignment shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Injection of 0.5 ng of pan-204 MO led to highly efficient suppression of mature mir-204 levels.
source: Injection of 0.5 ng of pan-204 MO led to highly efficient suppression of mature mir-204 levels (Figure 2b).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: At the 0.5 ng dose of pan-204 MO there were no noticeable morphological anomalies.
source: At the 0.5 ng dose there were no noticeable morphological anomalies, although slightly higher doses (0.75 ng) resulted in some pericardial edema, jaw defects, mild microcephaly and reduced eye development (Figure 2—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: The manuscript describes observations of morphology at different MO doses, with images shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1c.

claim: Slightly higher doses (0.75 ng) of pan-204 MO resulted in some pericardial edema, jaw defects, mild microcephaly and reduced eye development.
source: At the 0.5 ng dose there were no noticeable morphological anomalies, although slightly higher doses (0.75 ng) resulted in some pericardial edema, jaw defects, mild microcephaly and reduced eye development (Figure 2—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: The manuscript describes observations of morphological defects at 0.75 ng dose, with images shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1c.

claim: Secondary sprouts in mir-204-deficient animals failed to stop at the horizontal myoseptum and form the parachordal line, but instead continued to grow dorsally and contributed to veins.
source: Although initial secondary sprout formation and dorsal growth was normal in mir-204-deficient animals, secondary sprouts in these animals failed to stop at the horizontal myoseptum and form the parachordal line, but instead continued to grow dorsally and contributed to veins (Figure 2d and Figure 2—video 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 2d and Figure 2—video 1.

claim: Pan-204 MO-injected animals formed parachordals in only about 2 segments per 10 somites at three dpf, compared to control animals that had parachordal lines in most somitic segments.
source: Examination of the parachordal line at three dpf (Figure 2e–h,m) showed that compared to control MO-injected animals that had parachordal lines in most somitic segments at this stage (Figure 2e,f,m), pan-204 MO-injected animals formed parachordals in only about 2 segments per 10 somites (Figure 2g,h,m).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging and quantification shown in Figure 2e-h,m.

claim: mir-204-deficient animals displayed nearly complete loss of thoracic duct formation at five dpf.
source: Similarly, examination of the thoracic duct at five dpf (Figure 2i–l,n) showed that control MO-injected animals had a thoracic duct in virtually all segments (Figure 2i,j,n) while mir-204-deficient animals displayed nearly complete loss of thoracic duct formation (Figure 2k,l,n).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging and quantification shown in Figure 2i-l,n.

claim: Injection of 0.5 ng of each individual MO (MO1, MO2, or MO3) alone did not affect lymphatic vessel development.
source: Injection of 0.5 ng of each individual MO alone did not affect lymphatic vessel development (Figure 2—figure supplement 1b–d,i).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging and quantification shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2b-d,i.

claim: Pairwise co-injection of 0.5 ng MO1 and 0.5 ng MO2 resulted in defective thoracic duct formation.
source: Pairwise co-injection of 0.5 ng MO1 and 0.5 ng MO2 resulted in defective thoracic duct formation (Figure 2—figure supplement 2e,j), but pairwise co-injection of either MO1 + MO3 or MO2 + MO3 did not affect lymphatic vessel formation (Figure 2—figure supplement 2f,g,j).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging and quantification shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2e,j.

claim: Pairwise co-injection of either MO1 + MO3 or MO2 + MO3 did not affect lymphatic vessel formation.
source: Pairwise co-injection of 0.5 ng MO1 and 0.5 ng MO2 resulted in defective thoracic duct formation (Figure 2—figure supplement 2e,j), but pairwise co-injection of either MO1 + MO3 or MO2 + MO3 did not affect lymphatic vessel formation (Figure 2—figure supplement 2f,g,j).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging and quantification shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2f,g,j.

claim: Animals injected with 0.5 ng of each of the three MOs (MO1, MO2, and MO3) had lymphatic defects similar to but no more severe than animals injected with either the MO1 + MO2 combination or 0.5 ng of pan-204 MO.
source: Animals injected with 0.5 ng of each of the three MOs (MO1, MO2, and MO3, for a total of 1.5 ng injected) had lymphatic defects similar to but no more severe than animals injected with either the MO1 + MO2 combination or 0.5 ng of pan-204 MO (Figure 2—figure supplement 2h,j and Figure 2n).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging and quantification shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2h,j and Figure 2n.

claim: mir-204-1 and mir-204-2 play relatively more important roles than mir-204-3 during lymphatic development.
source: These results suggest that mir-204–1 and mir-204–2 play relatively more important roles than mir-204–3 during lymphatic development, and confirm that suppressing mir-204 function leads to defective lymphatic vessel formation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the differential effects of various MO combinations on lymphatic development.

claim: A 22 bp CRISPR/Cas9 mir-204-1 deletion mutant was isolated that deletes the majority of the mature mir-204 sequence (17 out of 22 nt) and the entire seed sequence.
source: Using an active single guide RNA (sgRNA) targeting mir-204–1 (Figure 3a), we isolated a 22 bp CRISPR/Cas9 mir-204–1 deletion mutant that deletes the majority of the mature mir-204 sequence (17 out of 22 nt) and the entire seed sequence at this locus (Figure 3b).
evidence: The manuscript describes the generation and characterization of the mir-204-1 mutant, with sequence alignment shown in Figure 3b.

claim: mir-204-1 homozygous mutants showed only an approximately 20% decrease in mir-204 levels compared to wildtype embryos.
source: Only an approximately 20% decrease in mir-204 levels in mir-204–1 homozygous mutants (miR-204–1-/-) compared to wildtype embryos suggests that reduction from mir-204–1 loss is compensated for by mir-204–2 and/or mir-204–3 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1a.

claim: The mir-204-1-/- animals were viable and fertile and did not have obvious morphological defects up to adulthood.
source: The mir-204–1-/- animals were viable and fertile and did not have obvious morphological defects up to adulthood (Figure 3c,d and data not shown).
evidence: The manuscript describes observations of mir-204-1-/- mutant viability and morphology, with images shown in Figure 3c,d.

claim: mir-204-1-/- mutant animals injected with MO2 fail to properly form the thoracic duct and other lymphatic vessels.
source: Entirely consistent with the data generated exclusively using morpholinos (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), mir-204–1-/- mutant animals injected with either MO2 (Figure 3e,h) or with MO2+MO3 (Figure 3g,h) fail to properly form the thoracic duct and other lymphatic vessels, but mir-204–1-/- mutants injected with MO3 developed normal lymphatics (Figure 3f,h).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging and quantification shown in Figure 3e,h.

claim: mir-204-1-/- mutant animals injected with MO2+MO3 fail to properly form the thoracic duct and other lymphatic vessels.
source: Entirely consistent with the data generated exclusively using morpholinos (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), mir-204–1-/- mutant animals injected with either MO2 (Figure 3e,h) or with MO2+MO3 (Figure 3g,h) fail to properly form the thoracic duct and other lymphatic vessels, but mir-204–1-/- mutants injected with MO3 developed normal lymphatics (Figure 3f,h).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging and quantification shown in Figure 3g,h.

claim: mir-204-1-/- mutants injected with MO3 developed normal lymphatics.
source: Entirely consistent with the data generated exclusively using morpholinos (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), mir-204–1-/- mutant animals injected with either MO2 (Figure 3e,h) or with MO2+MO3 (Figure 3g,h) fail to properly form the thoracic duct and other lymphatic vessels, but mir-204–1-/- mutants injected with MO3 developed normal lymphatics (Figure 3f,h).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging and quantification shown in Figure 3f,h.

claim: MO2-injected mir-204-1-/- mutant animals showed defects in parachordal line formation.
source: MO2-injected mir-204–1-/- mutant animals also showed defects in earlier parachordal line formation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1b–d), like pan-204 MO-injected animals (Figure 2g,h,m).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging and quantification shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1b-d.

claim: Suppressing biogenesis of mir-204 from the mir-204-1 and mir-204-2 loci is sufficient to disrupt mir-204 function in lymphatic vessel formation.
source: These data indicate that suppressing biogenesis of mir-204 from the mir-204–1 and mir-204–2 loci is sufficient to disrupt mir-204 function in lymphatic vessel formation, regardless of whether a genetic mutant or morpholino is used to suppress miR-204–1.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined results of genetic mutant and morpholino experiments.

claim: mir-204 triple homozygous mutants showed strongly reduced expression of mir-204.
source: Although expression of mir-204 was strongly reduced in mir-204 triple homozygous mutants (Figure 3—figure supplement 2b), they did not display statistically significant lymphatic defects (Figure 3—figure supplement 2c–e), presumably due to an unknown compensatory mechanism taking place in animals where all genomic mature mir-204 sequences are defective.
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2b.

claim: mir-204 triple homozygous mutants did not display statistically significant lymphatic defects.
source: Although expression of mir-204 was strongly reduced in mir-204 triple homozygous mutants (Figure 3—figure supplement 2b), they did not display statistically significant lymphatic defects (Figure 3—figure supplement 2c–e), presumably due to an unknown compensatory mechanism taking place in animals where all genomic mature mir-204 sequences are defective.
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2c-e.

claim: Embryos injected with mrc1a:mir204-eGFP formed a significantly increased number of thoracic duct segments at three dpf compared to control embryos.
source: In comparison to control embryos that were just beginning thoracic duct formation (Figure 4b), embryos injected with mrc1a:mir204-eGFP formed a significantly increased number of thoracic duct segments (Figure 4c) suggesting that endothelial expression of mir-204 promotes early thoracic duct development (Figure 4d).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging and quantification shown in Figure 4b-d.

claim: Germline transgenic progeny carrying Tg(mrc1a:mir204-egfp) display precocious development of the thoracic duct.
source: Similar to the results from the mosaic analysis, germline transgenic progeny generated from these fish display precocious development of the thoracic duct (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a–c).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging and quantification shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1a-c.

claim: Tg(mrc1a:mir204-egfp) animals are viable and fertile with no obvious morphological abnormalities or other defects.
source: These animals are viable and fertile with no obvious morphological abnormalities or other defects, including normal stage-specific spacing between the dorsal aorta and posterior cardinal vein (Figure 4—figure supplement 1d), despite an approximately 2-fold increase in mature miR-204 levels measured by qPCR at three dpf (Figure 4—figure supplement 1e).
evidence: The manuscript describes observations of transgenic animal viability and morphology, with quantification shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1d.

claim: Tg(mrc1a:mir204-egfp) animals have an approximately 2-fold increase in mature miR-204 levels at three dpf.
source: These animals are viable and fertile with no obvious morphological abnormalities or other defects, including normal stage-specific spacing between the dorsal aorta and posterior cardinal vein (Figure 4—figure supplement 1d), despite an approximately 2-fold increase in mature miR-204 levels measured by qPCR at three dpf (Figure 4—figure supplement 1e).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1e.

claim: Increased endothelial mir-204 expression specifically promotes early lymphatic development.
source: These results suggest that increased endothelial mir-204 expression specifically promotes early lymphatic development.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the precocious thoracic duct development observed in transgenic animals overexpressing mir-204.

claim: The loss-of-lymphatic phenotype in MO2-injected mir-204-1-/- embryos was rescued by co-injection of the mrc1a:miR204-eGFP transgene.
source: MO2-injected mir-204–1-/- embryos showed strong suppression of thoracic duct formation (Figure 4e,h,k), but this was rescued by co-injection of the mrc1a:miR204-eGFP transgene (Figure 4f,g,i,j,k), with stronger 'rescue' noted in animals with a higher mosaic contribution from the transgene (Figure 4g,j,k).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging and quantification shown in Figure 4e-k.

claim: Endothelial-autonomous miR-204 function is required for developmental lymphangiogenesis.
source: Together, these data indicate that endothelial-autonomous miR-204 function is required for developmental lymphangiogenesis.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the rescue experiments showing that endothelial-specific mir-204 expression can restore lymphatic development in mir-204-deficient animals.

claim: Human NFATC1 contains a putative miR-204 binding site in its 3'UTR.
source: Human NFATC1 contains a putative miR-204 binding site in its 3'UTR (Figure 5a).
evidence: The manuscript describes the identification of a miR-204 binding site in the NFATC1 3'UTR, with sequence alignment shown in Figure 5a.

claim: Luciferase reporter activity containing the NFATC1 3'UTR was significantly suppressed in the presence of miR-204 but not in the presence of miR-126 control.
source: Luciferase reporter activity was significantly suppressed in the presence of miR-204 but not in the presence of the miR-126 control (Figure 5b).
evidence: The claim is supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 5b.

claim: Mutating four nucleotides in the seed binding sequence of the NFATC1 3'UTR rendered the construct insensitive to suppression by miR-204.
source: To confirm the specificity of NFATC1 miR-204 target site recognition, we mutated four nucleotides in the seed binding sequence of the NFATC1 3'UTR (Figure 5a) and demonstrated that this rendered the construct insensitive to suppression by miR-204 (Figure 5b), confirming that this binding site is critical for direct targeting.
evidence: The claim is supported by luciferase reporter assay data with mutated constructs shown in Figure 5b.

claim: Overexpression of miR-204 in human LECs suppressed endogenous NFATC1 expression.
source: Overexpression of miR-204 in human LECs suppressed endogenous NFATC1 expression while miR-204 inhibitor (antagomir) increased endogenous NFATC1 expression, showing that miR-204 also regulates endogenous NFATC1 transcript levels in human LEC (Figure 5c).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 5c.

claim: miR-204 inhibitor (antagomir) increased endogenous NFATC1 expression in human LECs.
source: Overexpression of miR-204 in human LECs suppressed endogenous NFATC1 expression while miR-204 inhibitor (antagomir) increased endogenous NFATC1 expression, showing that miR-204 also regulates endogenous NFATC1 transcript levels in human LEC (Figure 5c).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 5c.

claim: Zebrafish nfatc1 contains a mir-204 binding site in its 3'UTR.
source: Zebrafish nfatc1 also contains a mir-204 binding site in its 3'UTR (Figure 5d).
evidence: The manuscript describes the identification of a mir-204 binding site in the zebrafish nfatc1 3'UTR, with sequence alignment shown in Figure 5d.

claim: The activity of a luciferase reporter containing the zebrafish nfatc1 3'UTR is strongly suppressed by miR-204.
source: The activity of a luciferase reporter containing the zebrafish nfatc1 3'UTR is also strongly suppressed by miR-204, and this suppression is fully rescued by mutating the seed binding sequence in the nfatc1 3'UTR (Figure 5e).
evidence: The claim is supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 5e.

claim: Suppression of miR-204 by mutating the seed binding sequence in the zebrafish nfatc1 3'UTR fully rescued the suppression by miR-204.
source: The activity of a luciferase reporter containing the zebrafish nfatc1 3'UTR is also strongly suppressed by miR-204, and this suppression is fully rescued by mutating the seed binding sequence in the nfatc1 3'UTR (Figure 5e).
evidence: The claim is supported by luciferase reporter assay data with mutated constructs shown in Figure 5e.

claim: mir-204 knockdown using the pan-204 MO results in increased levels of endogenous nfatc1 transcript in five dpf zebrafish embryos.
source: Importantly, mir-204 knockdown using the pan-204 MO (targeting all three zebrafish mir-204s) results in increased levels of endogenous nfatc1 transcript in five dpf zebrafish embryos (Figure 5f).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 5f.

claim: miR-204-mediated regulation of NFATC1 is conserved between human and zebrafish.
source: Together, these data demonstrate conserved miR-204-mediated regulation of NFATC1.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the luciferase and qPCR data showing miR-204 regulation of NFATC1 in both human and zebrafish.

claim: Loss of Nfatc1 in mice is associated with lymphatic hyperplasia.
source: As noted above, loss of Nfatc1 in mice is associated with lymphatic hyperplasia (Norrmén et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is based on a citation to previous work by Norrmén et al., 2009.

claim: Knockdown of nfatc1 in zebrafish using two different morpholinos causes thoracic duct enlargement.
source: Using two different morpholinos targeting nfatc1 (splice MO and ATG MO), we show that knockdown of this gene in the zebrafish also causes thoracic duct enlargement, similar to that shown in mice, with no noticeable abnormal blood vessel formation (Figure 6a–e and Figure 6—figure supplement 1a–e).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging and quantification shown in Figure 6a-e and Figure 6—figure supplement 1a-e.

claim: Zebrafish larvae treated with a low dose of CsA (1 ug/mL) displayed thoracic duct enlargement phenotype observed in nfatc1 MO-injected animals.
source: The zebrafish larvae treated with a low doses of CsA (1 ug/mL) also displayed thoracic duct enlargement phenotype observed in nfatc1 MO-injected animals (Figure 6—figure supplement 1f–j).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging and quantification shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1f-j.

claim: nfatc1△8/△8 mutants had enlarged thoracic ducts at five dpf.
source: Like nfatc1 morphants and CsA-treated animals, nfatc1△8/△8 mutants also had enlarged thoracic ducts at five dpf (Figure 6g–k).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging and quantification shown in Figure 6g-k.

claim: nfatc1 is required for proper lymphatic development in the zebrafish.
source: Therefore, consistent with previous data in mice, our results suggest that nfatc1 is required for proper lymphatic development in the zebrafish.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the lymphatic defects observed in nfatc1 morphants, CsA-treated animals, and nfatc1 mutants.

claim: In animals co-injected with both pan-204 MO and nfatc1 splice MO, formation of the thoracic duct is largely restored.
source: However, in animals co-injected with both pan-204 MO and nfatc1 splice MO, formation of the thoracic duct is largely restored (Figure 7c,f,j), as is the formation other lymphatic vessels including the DLLV and intersegmental lymphatics (ISLV) (Figure 7c,i,k).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging and quantification shown in Figure 7c,f,j.

claim: In animals co-injected with both pan-204 MO and nfatc1 splice MO, formation of the DLLV and intersegmental lymphatics is restored.
source: However, in animals co-injected with both pan-204 MO and nfatc1 splice MO, formation of the thoracic duct is largely restored (Figure 7c,f,j), as is the formation other lymphatic vessels including the DLLV and intersegmental lymphatics (ISLV) (Figure 7c,i,k).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging and quantification shown in Figure 7c,i,k.

claim: Abnormal lymphatic vessel development in mir-204 deficient animals can be substantially rescued by suppressing nfatc1 expression.
source: These results suggest that abnormal lymphatic vessel development in mir-204 deficient animals can be substantially rescued by suppressing nfatc1 expression.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the rescue experiments showing that nfatc1 knockdown restores lymphatic development in mir-204-deficient animals.

claim: A proper balance between mir-204 and nfatc1 is critical for proper lymphatic vessel development.
source: Based on all of our findings, we propose that a proper balance between mir-204 and nfatc1 is critical for proper lymphatic vessel development, with loss of either mir-204 or nfatc1 causing defects in lymphatic vessel formation (Figure 7l).
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from all the experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: Loss of either mir-204 or nfatc1 causes defects in lymphatic vessel formation.
source: Based on all of our findings, we propose that a proper balance between mir-204 and nfatc1 is critical for proper lymphatic vessel development, with loss of either mir-204 or nfatc1 causing defects in lymphatic vessel formation (Figure 7l).
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from all the experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: The lymphatic system is important for fluid and protein homeostasis, lipid transport, and immunity.
source: The lymphatic system is important for fluid and protein homeostasis, lipid transport, and immunity.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about the lymphatic system.

claim: Lymphatic malfunction is linked to many pathologies including lymphedema, cancer metastasis, and cardiovascular disease.
source: Lymphatic malfunction is linked to many pathologies including lymphedema, cancer metastasis, and cardiovascular disease (Petrova and Koh, 2018; Venero Galanternik et al., 2016; Alitalo, 2011; Stacker et al., 2014; Lim et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Primitive lymphatic vessels are derived from lymphatic endothelial cell (LEC) progenitors that transdifferentiate from venous blood endothelial cells (BECs) and subsequently migrate away from the veins to form lymphatic vessels.
source: Primitive lymphatic vessels are derived from lymphatic endothelial cell (LEC) progenitors that transdifferentiate from venous blood endothelial cells (BECs) and subsequently migrate away from the veins to form lymphatic vessels (Sabin, 1902; Hong et al., 2002; Koltowska et al., 2013; Nicenboim et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: PROX1, SOX18, COUPTFII, VEGFC/VEGFR3, NRP2, CCBE1, CLEC2, YAP/TAZ, and NFATC1 are required for proper regulation of lymphangiogenesis during development and disease.
source: A variety of factors have been identified that are required for proper regulation of lymphangiogenesis during development and disease, including PROX1, SOX18, COUPTFII, VEGFC/VEGFR3, NRP2, CCBE1, CLEC2, YAP/TAZ, and NFATC1 (Wigle and Oliver, 1999; Dumont et al., 1998; Karkkainen et al., 2004; François et al., 2008; Srinivasan et al., 2010; Yuan et al., 2002; Uhrin et al., 2010; Hogan et al., 2009; Kulkarni et al., 2009; Sweet et al., 2015; Bui et al., 2016; Cho et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: The development of the zebrafish lymphatic vascular system is highly conserved and stereotyped.
source: The development of the zebrafish lymphatic vascular system is highly conserved and stereotyped (Yaniv et al., 2006; Okuda et al., 2012; Jung et al., 2017; Küchler et al., 2006), and the availability of transgenic zebrafish expressing fluorescent reporters in lymphatic endothelium makes it straightforward to monitor lymphatic development at the single cell level in vivo and visualize even subtle lymphatic defects using optimized high-resolution microscopy technologies (Jung et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: MicroRNAs are important posttranscriptional regulators that play crucial roles in developmental, physiological, and disease-related processes in animals.
source: MicroRNAs are important posttranscriptional regulators that play crucial roles in developmental, physiological, and disease-related processes in animals (Gebert and MacRae, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: MicroRNAs are noncoding RNAs approximately 22 nucleotide long that guide Argonaute proteins for gene silencing by mRNA degradation and/or translational repression.
source: They are noncoding RNAs approximately 22 nucleotide long that guide Argonaute proteins for gene silencing by mRNA degradation and/or translational repression (Jonas and Izaurralde, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Targeting of microRNAs is accomplished by binding of the key nucleotides 2-8 (the 'seed' sequence) and additional microRNA sequences to complementary sequences in target mRNAs.
source: Targeting of microRNAs is accomplished by binding of the key nucleotides 2–8 (the 'seed' sequence) and additional microRNA sequences to complementary sequences in target mRNAs (Bartel, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The majority of microRNA target sites are located in the 3' untranslated regions (UTRs) of mRNAs.
source: The majority of microRNA target sites are located in the 3' untranslated regions (UTRs) of mRNAs, although some microRNA targeting also occurs in 5'UTR and coding sequences (Tay et al., 2008; Lytle et al., 2007; Jung et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Some microRNA targeting occurs in 5'UTR and coding sequences.
source: The majority of microRNA target sites are located in the 3' untranslated regions (UTRs) of mRNAs, although some microRNA targeting also occurs in 5'UTR and coding sequences (Tay et al., 2008; Lytle et al., 2007; Jung et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: MicroRNA regulatory networks are thought to confer robustness to biological processes by reinforcing transcription programs and attenuating aberrant transcripts.
source: MicroRNA regulatory networks are thought to confer robustness to biological processes by reinforcing transcription programs and attenuating aberrant transcripts by either switching off or fine-tuning gene expression, helping to buffer against random fluctuations in transcript copy number (Ebert and Sharp, 2012; Staton et al., 2011; Choi et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: BEC-specific microRNAs such as miR-31 and miR-181a target Prox1 and prevent lymphatic specification in BECs.
source: Profiling of microRNAs in human lymphatic endothelial cells (LECs) and blood endothelial cells (BECs) has identified BEC-specific microRNAs such as miR-31 and miR-181a that target Prox1 and prevent lymphatic specification in BECs (Leslie Pedrioli et al., 2010; Kazenwadel et al., 2010; Dunworth et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Some microRNAs can help BECs retain their identity by negatively regulating lymphatic development.
source: These studies suggest some microRNAs can help BECs retain their identity by negatively regulating lymphatic development.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the studies showing BEC-specific microRNAs target lymphatic genes.

claim: Manipulation of endothelial microRNAs has been shown to result in defective lymphatic development.
source: Manipulation of endothelial microRNAs has also been shown to result in defective lymphatic development (Kontarakis et al., 2018; Nicoli et al., 2012; Chen et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The majority of the 30 highly significantly LEC-enriched microRNAs identified were specific to mammals.
source: The majority of the 30 highly significantly LEC-enriched microRNAs we identified were specific to mammals, with only seven microRNAs conserved in other vertebrate species.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of the sequencing data and conservation of the identified microRNAs.

claim: Only seven of the 30 highly significantly LEC-enriched microRNAs are conserved in other vertebrate species.
source: The majority of the 30 highly significantly LEC-enriched microRNAs we identified were specific to mammals, with only seven microRNAs conserved in other vertebrate species.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of the sequencing data and conservation of the identified microRNAs.

claim: Most LEC microRNAs have diverged and/or evolved for mammalian-specific functions.
source: This suggests that most of these LEC microRNAs have diverged and/or evolved for mammalian-specific functions.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that most LEC-enriched microRNAs are mammal-specific.

claim: miR-204 plays an important conserved role during lymphatic development.
source: The most highly LEC-enriched microRNA was miR-204, a microRNA with 100% sequence identity across a broad swath of vertebrate species (Figure 2—figure supplement 2a), suggesting it plays an important conserved role during lymphatic development.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the high conservation of miR-204 sequence across vertebrates.

claim: The study also uncovered microRNAs such as miR-326, miR-139, miR-338, miR-148a, and miR-30d that had been previously reported to be LEC-enriched.
source: In addition to miR-204 and a number of other newly identified LEC-enriched microRNAs, we also uncovered microRNAs such as miR-326, miR-139, miR-338, miR-148a, and miR-30d that had been previously reported to be LEC-enriched (Leslie Pedrioli et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is based on comparison with previous studies, supported by a citation.

claim: miR-204 was not identified in the previous study by Pedrioli et al, despite its being the most highly enriched lymphatic microRNA in the current study.
source: Intriguingly, miR-204 was not identified in the previous study by Pedrioli et al, despite its being the most highly enriched lymphatic microRNA in our study, while the most enriched LEC microRNA reported by Pedrioli et al, miR-95, was excluded from our analysis due to a low number of sequence reads.
evidence: The claim is based on comparison with previous studies.

claim: The most enriched LEC microRNA reported by Pedrioli et al, miR-95, was excluded from the current analysis due to a low number of sequence reads.
source: Intriguingly, miR-204 was not identified in the previous study by Pedrioli et al, despite its being the most highly enriched lymphatic microRNA in our study, while the most enriched LEC microRNA reported by Pedrioli et al, miR-95, was excluded from our analysis due to a low number of sequence reads.
evidence: The claim is based on the filtering criteria applied to the sequencing data.

claim: The disparate results between the current study and that of Pedrioli et al. may reflect differences in the starting material for sequencing, the profiling methods used, or the bioinformatic tools and filters employed.
source: The reasons for the disparate results obtained from our data set and that of Pedrioli et al. are not clear, but they may reflect differences in the starting material for sequencing, the profiling methods used, or the bioinformatic tools and filters employed.
evidence: The claim is speculation about possible reasons for differences between studies.

claim: The current study used three biological replicates for both the LEC and BEC sequencing.
source: We would note that out study used three biological replicates for both the LEC and BEC sequencing, and that we sequenced to a relatively high depth and applied very stringent filtering to our data set.
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental design of the sequencing study.

claim: The current study sequenced to a relatively high depth and applied very stringent filtering to the data set.
source: We would note that out study used three biological replicates for both the LEC and BEC sequencing, and that we sequenced to a relatively high depth and applied very stringent filtering to our data set.
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental design and data analysis approach.

claim: The remarkable evolutionary conservation of the miR-204 sequence throughout the vertebrates suggests that this microRNA likely plays an important conserved function.
source: The remarkable evolutionary conservation of the miR-204 sequence throughout the vertebrates suggests that this microRNA likely plays an important conserved function.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the high conservation of miR-204 sequence.

claim: Suppression of mir-204 leads to strong defects in developmental lymphangiogenesis in zebrafish.
source: Indeed, our zebrafish findings show that suppression of mir-204 leads to strong defects in developmental lymphangiogenesis.
evidence: The claim is based on the morpholino and genetic mutant experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: Human miR-204 is encoded by only a single locus in intron 6 of the TRPM3 gene.
source: Although the sequence of mature zebrafish mir-204 is identical to human miR-204, human miR-204 is encoded by only a single locus in intron 6 of the TRPM3 gene, while zebrafish mir-204 is encoded by three separate loci within the introns of the trpm3, trpm1a, and trpm1b genes.
evidence: The manuscript describes the genomic organization of miR-204 in humans and zebrafish.

claim: The mammalian TRPM1 gene has a related microRNA encoded within a similar intron to zebrafish trpm1a and trpm1b, that may have evolved from mir-204.
source: Interestingly, however, the mammalian TRPM1 gene has a related microRNA encoded within a similar intron to zebrafish trpm1a and trpm1b, that may have evolved from mir-204.
evidence: The claim is speculation about the evolutionary relationship between miR-204 and miR-211.

claim: The essential role of miR-204 in developmental lymphangiogenesis was demonstrated using multiple complementary loss-of-function approaches.
source: We demonstrated the essential role of miR-204 in developmental lymphangiogenesis using multiple complementary loss-of-function approaches, including (i) a 'pan-204' morpholino targeting the mature mir-204 sequence produced by all three zebrafish mir-204 loci, (ii) morpholinos individually targeting sequences required for the maturation of each of the three zebrafish mir-204's (MO1, MO2, and MO3), and (iii) a CRISPR-Cas9-generated genetic mutant ablating the mir-204–1 locus, which caused a lymphatic defect in combination with MO2 (targeting miR-204–2).
evidence: The claim summarizes the multiple experimental approaches used to study miR-204 function.

claim: Treatments that target at minimum mir-204-1 and mir-204-2 result in comparable dramatic loss-of-lymphatic phenotypes.
source: Our results revealed that treatments that target at minimum mir-204–1 and mir-204–2 result in comparable dramatic loss-of-lymphatic phenotypes, including loss of the parachordal line at three dpf and loss of the thoracic duct and other trunk lymphatic vessels at five dpf.
evidence: The claim summarizes the results from the various loss-of-function experiments.

claim: The mrc1a:mir204-1-eGFP transgene 'rescues' thoracic duct formation when introduced into miR-204-1-/- mutants injected with MO2.
source: Importantly, the mrc1a:mir204-1-eGFP transgene also 'rescues' thoracic duct formation when introduced into miR-204–1-/- mutants injected with MO2 (targeting miR-204–2) that would otherwise lack lymphatics, demonstrating that re-introduction of miR-204 exclusively in the endothelium is sufficient to restore normal lymphatic development in miR-204-deficient animals.
evidence: The claim is based on the rescue experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: Re-introduction of miR-204 exclusively in the endothelium is sufficient to restore normal lymphatic development in miR-204-deficient animals.
source: Importantly, the mrc1a:mir204-1-eGFP transgene also 'rescues' thoracic duct formation when introduced into miR-204–1-/- mutants injected with MO2 (targeting miR-204–2) that would otherwise lack lymphatics, demonstrating that re-introduction of miR-204 exclusively in the endothelium is sufficient to restore normal lymphatic development in miR-204-deficient animals.
evidence: The claim is based on the rescue experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: Triple mutants disrupting all three zebrafish miR-204 loci do not display a significantly measurable lymphatic defect.
source: Despite all of these interlocking findings strongly arguing for a key role for miR-204 in lymphatic development, triple mutants disrupting all three zebrafish miR-204 loci do not display a significantly measurable lymphatic defect.
evidence: The claim is based on the analysis of triple mutants shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: There is precedent in the literature for zebrafish microRNA mutants failing to exhibit the full phenotypes noted in microRNA knockdown studies.
source: Although the reasons for this are unclear, there is precedent in the literature for zebrafish microRNA mutants failing to exhibit the full phenotypes noted in microRNA knockdown studies.
evidence: The claim is based on knowledge of previous studies in the field.

claim: Suppression of mir-126 causes blood vessel defects in mir-126 morpholino-injected animals.
source: Suppression of the evolutionarily conserved endothelial-enriched microRNA mir-126 causes blood vessels defects in mir-126 morpholino-injected animals (Fish et al., 2008) (Zou et al., 2011), although lower dose morpholino injections cause mainly lymphatic defects with relatively minor effects on blood vessels (Chen et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Lower dose mir-126 morpholino injections cause mainly lymphatic defects with relatively minor effects on blood vessels.
source: Suppression of the evolutionarily conserved endothelial-enriched microRNA mir-126 causes blood vessels defects in mir-126 morpholino-injected animals (Fish et al., 2008) (Zou et al., 2011), although lower dose morpholino injections cause mainly lymphatic defects with relatively minor effects on blood vessels (Chen et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: mir-126 mutant zebrafish lack the vascular phenotype described in previous morpholino studies and display only the defects in lymphatic vessel development seen with partial knockdowns.
source: Interestingly, mir-126 mutant zebrafish also lack the vascular phenotype described in the previous morpholino studies and display only the defects in lymphatic vessel development seen with partial knockdowns (Kontarakis et al., 2018), suggesting compensation may be taking place in miR-126 mutants.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Compensation may be taking place in miR-126 mutants.
source: Interestingly, mir-126 mutant zebrafish also lack the vascular phenotype described in the previous morpholino studies and display only the defects in lymphatic vessel development seen with partial knockdowns (Kontarakis et al., 2018), suggesting compensation may be taking place in miR-126 mutants.
evidence: The claim is speculation based on the discrepancy between morpholino and mutant phenotypes.

claim: NFATC1 is important for lymphatic vessel development.
source: Previous studies have shown that the Nuclear Factor of Activated T-cells (NFAT) protein family member NFATC1 is important for lymphatic vessel development (Norrmén et al., 2009; Kulkarni et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Nfatc1 is co-expressed with Prox1-, Vegfr3-, and Pdpn-positive LEC progenitors originating from the cardinal vein.
source: Nfatc1 is co-expressed with Prox1-, Vegfr3-, and Pdpn-positive LEC progenitors originating from the cardinal vein indicating their potential involvement in lymphatic specification, and Nfatc1 null mice develop lymphatic hyperplasia suggesting a role in lymphatic maturation (Norrmén et al., 2009; Kulkarni et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Nfatc1 null mice develop lymphatic hyperplasia.
source: Nfatc1 is co-expressed with Prox1-, Vegfr3-, and Pdpn-positive LEC progenitors originating from the cardinal vein indicating their potential involvement in lymphatic specification, and Nfatc1 null mice develop lymphatic hyperplasia suggesting a role in lymphatic maturation (Norrmén et al., 2009; Kulkarni et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: NFATC1 was identified as a probable miR-204 target based on conserved miR-204 binding sites in the 3' UTRs of both human and zebrafish NFATC1 transcripts.
source: We identified NFATC1 as a probable miR-204 target based on conserved miR-204 binding sites in the 3' UTRs of both human and zebrafish NFATC1 transcripts and the expression of NFATC1 was suppressed by miR-204 mimic and increased by miR-204 antagomir in human LECs.
evidence: The claim is based on bioinformatic analysis and experimental validation.

claim: The expression of NFATC1 was suppressed by miR-204 mimic in human LECs.
source: We identified NFATC1 as a probable miR-204 target based on conserved miR-204 binding sites in the 3' UTRs of both human and zebrafish NFATC1 transcripts and the expression of NFATC1 was suppressed by miR-204 mimic and increased by miR-204 antagomir in human LECs.
evidence: The claim is based on qPCR data shown in Figure 5c.

claim: The expression of NFATC1 was increased by miR-204 antagomir in human LECs.
source: We identified NFATC1 as a probable miR-204 target based on conserved miR-204 binding sites in the 3' UTRs of both human and zebrafish NFATC1 transcripts and the expression of NFATC1 was suppressed by miR-204 mimic and increased by miR-204 antagomir in human LECs.
evidence: The claim is based on qPCR data shown in Figure 5c.

claim: Targeting of the NFATC1 3' UTR by miR-204 was verified using firefly/renilla dual luciferase NFATC1 3' UTR reporter assays.
source: We were able to verify targeting of the NFATC1 3' UTR by miR-204 using firefly/renilla dual luciferase NFATC1 3' UTR reporter assays, and demonstrate up-regulation of zebrafish nfatc1 upon mir-204 knockdown, confirming that miR-204 suppresses NFATC1 levels in vivo.
evidence: The claim is based on luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 5b and 5e.

claim: Zebrafish nfatc1 is up-regulated upon mir-204 knockdown.
source: We were able to verify targeting of the NFATC1 3' UTR by miR-204 using firefly/renilla dual luciferase NFATC1 3' UTR reporter assays, and demonstrate up-regulation of zebrafish nfatc1 upon mir-204 knockdown, confirming that miR-204 suppresses NFATC1 levels in vivo.
evidence: The claim is based on qPCR data shown in Figure 5f.

claim: miR-204 suppresses NFATC1 levels in vivo.
source: We were able to verify targeting of the NFATC1 3' UTR by miR-204 using firefly/renilla dual luciferase NFATC1 3' UTR reporter assays, and demonstrate up-regulation of zebrafish nfatc1 upon mir-204 knockdown, confirming that miR-204 suppresses NFATC1 levels in vivo.
evidence: The claim is based on the combined luciferase and qPCR data.

claim: Knocking down nfatc1 could rescue lymphatic development in mir-204-deficient zebrafish.
source: Finally, we showed that knocking down nfatc1 could rescue lymphatic development in mir-204-deficient zebrafish, suggesting that balanced expression of mir-204 and nfatc1 is critical for proper developmental lymphangiogenesis.
evidence: The claim is based on the rescue experiments shown in Figure 7.

claim: Balanced expression of mir-204 and nfatc1 is critical for proper developmental lymphangiogenesis.
source: Finally, we showed that knocking down nfatc1 could rescue lymphatic development in mir-204-deficient zebrafish, suggesting that balanced expression of mir-204 and nfatc1 is critical for proper developmental lymphangiogenesis.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the rescue experiments and the opposing effects of mir-204 and nfatc1 on lymphatic development.

claim: MicroRNAs often regulate many targets.
source: Since microRNAs often regulate many targets, and miR-204 does have potential target binding sites in other genes, further investigation will be required to characterize some of these additional genes and determine whether some of the lymphatic effects of miR-204 are mediated via regulation of other targets in addition to nfatc1.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about microRNA biology.

claim: miR-204 has potential target binding sites in other genes in addition to NFATC1.
source: Since microRNAs often regulate many targets, and miR-204 does have potential target binding sites in other genes, further investigation will be required to characterize some of these additional genes and determine whether some of the lymphatic effects of miR-204 are mediated via regulation of other targets in addition to nfatc1.
evidence: The claim is based on bioinformatic analysis of potential miR-204 targets.

claim: Further investigation will be required to determine whether some of the lymphatic effects of miR-204 are mediated via regulation of other targets in addition to nfatc1.
source: Since microRNAs often regulate many targets, and miR-204 does have potential target binding sites in other genes, further investigation will be required to characterize some of these additional genes and determine whether some of the lymphatic effects of miR-204 are mediated via regulation of other targets in addition to nfatc1.
evidence: This is a statement about future research directions.

claim: NFATC1 has been shown to play an important role in lymphangiogenesis in mammals.
source: Nevertheless, since (i) NFATC1 has already been shown to play an important role in lymphangiogenesis in mammals, (ii) suppression of nfatc1 in the zebrafish causes lymphatic hyperplasia, and (iii) nfatc1 knockdown effectively rescues the effects of miR-204 knockdown, our results suggest that nfatc1 is a major, key downstream target regulated by miR-204 in developing lymphatic endothelial cells.
evidence: The claim is based on citations to previous work.

claim: nfatc1 is a major, key downstream target regulated by miR-204 in developing lymphatic endothelial cells.
source: Nevertheless, since (i) NFATC1 has already been shown to play an important role in lymphangiogenesis in mammals, (ii) suppression of nfatc1 in the zebrafish causes lymphatic hyperplasia, and (iii) nfatc1 knockdown effectively rescues the effects of miR-204 knockdown, our results suggest that nfatc1 is a major, key downstream target regulated by miR-204 in developing lymphatic endothelial cells.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined evidence of NFATC1's role in lymphangiogenesis, the zebrafish nfatc1 phenotype, and the rescue experiments.

claim: The work establishes an important role for miR-204 in regulating lymphatic vascular network formation during embryonic development via modulation of its conserved target NFATC1.
source: In summary, our work establishes an important role for miR-204 in regulating lymphatic vascular network formation during embryonic development via modulation of its conserved target NFATC1.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main findings of the study.

claim: The findings provide important new insight into the role of lymphatic-enriched microRNAs during developmental lymphangiogenesis.
source: Our findings provide important new insight into the role of lymphatic-enriched microRNAs during developmental lymphangiogenesis, and by unveiling microRNA-regulated pathways provide new opportunities to understand lymphatic development and associated disorders.
evidence: This is a statement about the significance of the findings.

claim: By unveiling microRNA-regulated pathways, the findings provide new opportunities to understand lymphatic development and associated disorders.
source: Our findings provide important new insight into the role of lymphatic-enriched microRNAs during developmental lymphangiogenesis, and by unveiling microRNA-regulated pathways provide new opportunities to understand lymphatic development and associated disorders.
evidence: This is a statement about the potential impact of the findings.
